content: The diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care (POC) HBV DNA assays was compared to laboratory-based nucleic acid testing (NAT) in a systematic review of 15 studies involving 8,791 participants. Six studies evaluated the Xpert HBV DNA assay, while nine assessed other POC assays, including HBV-LAMP, Duplex real-time RAA, HBV-MCDA-LFB, and Cas12a-DETECTR assays. Sample types varied, with six studies using plasma, seven using serum or plasma, and two using whole blood. Four studies used fresh samples, while eight used frozen samples. The pooled sensitivity and specificity of the Xpert assay were 96% (95% CI: 94–98%) and 98% (95% CI: 90–100%), respectively, compared to laboratory-based NAT. Other POC assays demonstrated similarly high diagnostic accuracy, with pooled sensitivity and specificity of 98% (95% CI: 94–99%) and 99% (95% CI: 93–100%), respectively. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate to high. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended POC molecular assays for rapid diagnosis in other diseases, such as rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (TB), multidrug-resistant TB, and early infant diagnosis of HIV. In 2021, WHO also endorsed POC RNA assays for early infant HIV diagnosis and routine viral load monitoring in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART). These recommendations were based on high-certainty evidence showing faster result delivery and earlier ART initiation. For example, infants tested with POC assays were eight times more likely to start treatment within 60 days of sample collection. Similarly, POC HIV RNA testing improved result turnaround times and clinical action for elevated viral loads compared to standard care. A systematic review of 45 studies on hepatitis C virus (HCV) care found that POC RNA testing reduced the time from antibody testing to treatment initiation and increased uptake of RNA testing and treatment, particularly in marginalized populations with high rates of loss to follow-up, such as people who inject drugs. This evidence, though indirect, supports the use of POC platforms to reduce delays between testing and clinical decision-making for treatment initiation. The WHO Guidelines Development Group recognized the limited access to laboratory-based HBV DNA NAT assays in resource-limited settings due to high costs and infrastructure requirements. The increased availability of POC platforms, already used for HIV, TB, and COVID-19, presents an opportunity to expand access to HBV DNA testing. The group conditionally recommended POC NAT assays as an alternative to laboratory-based NAT for measuring HBV DNA, based on moderate to high-certainty evidence of high diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity: 96–98%; specificity: 98–99%). A systematic review of seven studies found that POC DNA testing was associated with high uptake of viral load testing (89%, 95% CI: 55–100%) and treatment initiation (88%, 95% CI: 66–100%) among eligible individuals. The time from testing to result return and treatment initiation ranged from one to eight days, with fewer healthcare visits required. However, the evidence was rated as very low certainty due to serious risk of bias and indirectness. Key benefits of POC HBV DNA assays include their ability to be decentralized to lower-level healthcare facilities, ease of use, and suitability for single-test runs. They can expand access to HBV testing for treatment eligibility assessment, antiviral prophylaxis in pregnant women with high viral loads, and treatment monitoring, particularly in hard-to-reach settings with limited laboratory infrastructure. POC platforms are already in use for other infectious diseases, and their integration into existing systems could further expand access and improve efficiency. Challenges include limited test throughput compared to laboratory-based platforms, the need to prioritize testing in high-demand settings, and the limited number of manufacturers producing POC HBV NAT assays, which restricts competition and cost reduction. Additionally, some assays require high-temperature incineration for safe disposal of chemical waste. A multicountry survey of over 400 people with hepatitis B highlighted the importance of confidentiality, access to knowledgeable staff, appropriate counseling, and non-stigmatizing approaches in hepatitis B testing and treatment. Cost and availability were identified as major barriers to accessing HBV DNA testing, emphasizing the need for POC NAT assays as an alternative. POC HBV DNA assays can promote equity by improving access in high-risk populations, such as pregnant women in antenatal care, people in prisons, and individuals who inject drugs. The introduction of multi-disease testing devices offers additional opportunities for integration, cost savings, and expanded access. Countries with existing multi-disease platforms for HIV, TB, and COVID-19 can consider integrating HBV DNA testing into these systems. Implementation of POC testing requires strong decentralized systems, including quality control, platform maintenance, supply chain management, and trained personnel. Basic laboratory infrastructure, such as centrifuges and temperature-controlled environments, is essential. Regular calibration and quality assurance checks are necessary to maintain device validity and performance. Research gaps include the need for rigorous studies, ideally randomized controlled trials, to evaluate the use of POC platforms for hepatitis B treatment decisions and monitoring. Future studies should assess cost-effectiveness, utility in adolescents and children, and the integration of HBV DNA testing with other diseases like TB, HCV, and HIV. WHO now recommends reflex HBV DNA testing for individuals testing positive for HBsAg as an additional strategy to promote linkage to care and treatment. Reflex testing can be implemented through laboratory-based or clinic-based approaches, reducing the need for additional visits and blood draws. Reflex testing has been shown to increase HBV DNA testing uptake and reduce turnaround times to treatment initiation, with evidence suggesting it is cost-saving and feasible to implement, even in resource-limited settings.
